source.title: (tentatively) Found 600+ Monosemantic Features in a Small LM Using Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: The post reports exploratory sparse-autoencoder feature results, but does not test neuron-pole job shares, explanations on held-out activations, automated explanation scores, or neuron-based attribution graphs as described in the versions.
record.gate_note: The post reports results for sparse-autoencoder features in Pythia-70M, not an audit of neuron poles. It does not report the share of neuron poles with one or more jobs, or test any of the listed claim versions. The results below concern related feature interpretability only.
record.test_reason: The post trains sparse autoencoders on Pythia-70M layer-2 MLP activations and inspects the learned features. It reports no share of neurons or neuron poles with one job. It does not test explanations against held-out firing, use automated simulation scoring, or build neuron-based attribution graphs. Its neuron-basis comparison concerns a single, hand-picked feature. The post works inside a superposition framing (features as combinations of neurons) rather than testing whether neurons are already clean.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The author offers tentative evidence that SAE dictionaries learn meaningful features that are combinations of neurons, not just monosemantic neurons. The author calls for better metrics, broader checks and larger models.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains sparse autoencoders on Pythia-70M activations and investigates learned feature directions using examples and ablations; it does not use the neuron-pole audit or explanation-testing method described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The author reports that apparent feature polysemanticity varies with MCS and with the threshold used to count associated neuron activations.

fits_no_version.finding: A near-identity dictionary feature, essentially a single neuron, was inspected. The author could not form any hypothesis of its meaning. By contrast, SAE feature #52 spread over roughly 3–80 neurons and read as a LaTeX-$ detector.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Pythia-70M, some coherent features are distributed across many MLP neurons, while some individual neurons resist interpretation (anecdotal, hand-picked).

fits_no_version.finding: An SAE trained on Pythia-70M layer 2 mid-MLP activations learned 600+ features judged meaningful. Lower-MCS features looked more polysemantic or were dead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse-autoencoder features in Pythia-70M can include interpretable directions that combine multiple neurons.

record.problems: The post calls its findings tentative and says the feature case study could be cherry-picked. The review of the top 70 features was brief; most low-MCS features could not be checked because they were dead. The author says the feature metrics and generality require further work, and provides no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results were reported. The post's examples and figures without stated outcome details were not entered as separate rows.

untested.parts: Neuron job shares across other models, MoE models and scale.
InceptionV1 cat/car neuron, pose, recursive generalization.
Effect of architecture, regularization and tools on the share of interpretable neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Whether activating-example explanations predict firing elsewhere. The uniform-bin check applies to an SAE feature, not a neuron.
Automated simulation scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts are given because no row bears on any version. The author notes that meaningful monosemantic neurons also exist in the model, but gives no count or share.

versions.untested_parts: Comparisons across models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, and recursive generalization.
Architecture, regularization, and tool effects on interpretability shares; InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a trained replacement model.
Whether explanations derived from activating examples predict firing on examples they were not written from.
Automated simulation scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Trained a sparse autoencoder dictionary on layer 2 mid-MLP activations after GeLU.
rows.measure: Number of features the author says the resulting decoder learned
rows.note: The author says they expect around 8k–16k features to be learnable; this is not a measured neuron-pole job share.
rows.check: Counts SAE features, not neuron poles. The value is the author's tentative estimate, not a measured share.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Removed a context token and reran the model to measure the change in feature #52's activation at the final position.
rows.measure: Feature activation at the final position
rows.note: The author interprets the feature as detecting dollar signs used for LaTeX; this is a sparse-autoencoder feature, not a neuron-pole audit.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Subtracted feature #52's direction multiplied by its magnitude from the neuron activation and measured changes in output-token log probabilities.
rows.value: The author reports effects on LaTeX-related tokens, with log probabilities both increasing and decreasing; no numerical effect sizes stated.
rows.locator: Feature Case Study — Ablate Feature Direction
rows.note: The post describes a feature-direction intervention, not an intervention on an individual neuron.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Prepended every vocabulary token to “for all $” and compared the resulting feature activation.

conditions.value: “for all $” preceded by each vocabulary token

rows.value: The most-increasing tokens were described as ending-dollar LaTeX cases; 97 tokens were among the most-decreasing and were described as more related to the money sense of “$”. Numerical activation changes not stated.
rows.note: The text also says “sold” sharply reduces activation and combining math words increases it, without giving numeric values.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Manually reviewed high-MCS features and compared their activation and feature-vector effects with the neuron basis and an identity-like dictionary.

conditions.value: Top 70 high-MCS features; some comparisons across the top 50

rows.measure: Qualitative feature interpretations and number of neuron activations associated with features
rows.value: The author reports that the selected feature appeared to represent about 3 to 80 neurons depending on the threshold; most identity-like dictionary features correlated with only one neuron above 0.3. Lower-MCS features appeared more polysemantic, and the author could not check most low-MCS features because they were dead, usually with zero activations.
rows.locator: Comparing to the Neuron Basis; Range of MCS Features
rows.note: This is an exploratory comparison of learned features and neuron activations, not a measure of how many neuron poles have a single job.
rows.check: Neuron-basis comparison of one hand-picked feature plus top-50 MCS correlations. The author says the feature was chosen because it represents a polysemantic neuron, so it cannot estimate a neuron-level share.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
